CONGRANT.TITLE: CUE Ethics: Collaborative Research: An Adaptable Discipline-Relevant Introductory Sequence to Build Computational Skills
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Computational knowledge and skills have become essential to all disciplines and economic sectors.  The ubiquity of computing impacts how we educate and prepare the future workforce regardless of one’s chosen career pathway. Thus, it is imperative to develop non-CS undergraduate students’ essential skills in solving problems computationally in their discipline and in possessing knowledge of ethical concerns related to growing cyber threats and vulnerabilities. To address this need, three institutions of higher education are collaborating as a Networked Improvement Community [NIC]: The University of Texas at El Paso [UTEP], Texas A&M University Corpus Christi, and the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.  The aim of improvement at each institution is to raise non-CS students’ motivation to pursue knowledge of computational skills and become aware of ethical and security issues. The proposed project has three objectives to meet its goal of developing non-CS students’ skills for solving problems using computation:  (1) develop and refine outcome-focused, problem-based, discipline-relevant course modules for creating course sequences that are adaptable to varying institutional context and disciplinary degree programs; and (2) incorporate inclusive practices into delivery of the modules to retain and advance students in the computational sequence.

Intellectual Merit. UTEP is the lead institution and Alliance Backbone of the NSF-funded National CAHSI (Computing Alliance for Hispanic-Serving Institutions) INCLUDES Alliance. The Alliance aims to broaden participation of Hispanics in computing using the conditions of collective impact, an improvement science framework closely aligned with NICs. With its 12-year history of building and supporting academic partnerships, CAHSI and its Backbone team are well positioned to support the IHE partnership in the proposed work, which aligns with CAHSI’s mission of growing and sustaining a networked community focused on advancement of Hispanics in computing. The proposed project has defined a collection of modules focused on problem-solving, computational thinking, cybersecurity, and ethics that can be used to create a sequence for STEM, non-CS majors that is adaptable to local context. In addition, the Alliance Backbone will support the professional development of instructors involved in the project with evidence- and research-based inclusive practices, which are especially important for success of Hispanics and other individuals from underrepresented groups. Using the improvement science framework with feedback from the external evaluator, the investigators and STEM subject matter experts from the partner institutions will critically review and iteratively improve organizational structures, course modules, and sequences. The investigators have expertise in working with interdisciplinary projects and are committed to collaborate in refinement of a reconfigurable, introductory course sequence designed to prepare the future STEM workforce with computational knowledge and skills. 

Broader Impacts. The partner institutions are Hispanic-Serving Institutions [HSIs] with majority Hispanic populations. Working with non-CS departments, the project will serve a significant number of women who are over-represented in the partnerships’ STEM fields (other than Physics) involved in the project. This has potential to broaden participation of students from underrepresented groups in computing, a priority of the NSF. The proposed modules are adaptable across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. Because the Alliance operates as a network of networks, it has numerous outlets for disseminating modules to both Alliance institutions and other HSIs. One such outlet is the Alliance’s non-profit-organization partners, Excelencia in Education and Great Minds in STEM, that are national Hispanic organizations sharing a core purpose of increasing the number of Hispanics who are competitive in higher education generally and in computing specifically.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of Futuro: a Data Intensive and High Performance Computing Cluster for Integrated Research and Education
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The purpose of this project is acquiring Futuro, a computer cluster for high performance parallel computing. Futuro will enable computational science research projects and computer science education with impact in bioinformatics, data mining, pattern discovery, genetic data analysis, experimental astronomical physical, collaborative filtering, theory of computation, high dimensional visualization, and other computational areas. The project seeks to lay the foundation for a strong research and education integration centered on computer science in two minority-serving universities, UT-Brownsville and UT-Pan American.

CONGRANT.TITLE: "BPC-LSA: Scaling and Adapting CAHSI Initiatives (SACI)"
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The Computing Alliance of Hispanic-Serving Institutions (CAHSI) was formed in 2005 to increase the number of Hispanic students who complete undergraduate and graduate degrees in computer and information sciences and engineering. With funding from the National Science Foundation, this alliance of seven universities has developed and demonstrated the effectiveness of a series of initiatives in achieving this goal. Miami Dade College (MDC), California State University San Marco (CSUSM), and the University of Texas Pan-American (UTPA) will collaborate to implement BPC-LSA: Scaling and Adapting CAHSI Initiatives (SACI).

CONGRANT.TITLE: Microarray Image Analysis
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Microarrays, which allows the analysis of hybridization expressions of genes, have been one of the most widely used high-throughput technologies with many different applications. For example, to identify genes involved in agricultural experiments, to represent cancer taxonomy in biomedical studies, or to develop new drugs in the pharmacology discipline. Accurate microarray image analysis is very important since researchers trust in the information provided in these experiments and construct conclusions based on the results produced by the software responsible in reading the hybridized arrays.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Genetic Characterization of the Lower Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
In collaboration with researchers from the Psychiatric Genetics Research Center and Epidemiology and Biostatistics Department at UTHSCSA, we will merge all these genetic information into the Regional Academic Health Center
Medical Research Division in Edinburg, Texas (E-RAHC) Genetics Group database. Information on samples, families, and genotypes already performed on over 1500 subjects of Mexican or Mexican-American descent, as well as samples
from other ethnic groups already collected in the Lower Rio Grande Valley (LRGV), will be merged too. We will lead the development of this database and work with E-RAHC and UTHSCSA faculty to generate publications on the genetic
population structure of the U.S. Latino population and of the LRGV.
